Your Majestyes
Loyall Subject,
Servant and Herbarist,

John Parkinson.

And although by the revolution of time it hath changed the note (that is from a Physicall Garden of Simples, to a Theater of Plants) yet not the nature, yea rather it hath gained the more matter by the overture, that intending to exclude many of those things that were not proper for it, this including a toto genere, dici potertint. For finding in my Profession many slips and errors crept therein and incident thereto, it stirred up a desire in me, having rightly weighed them, seriously to consider how such a customary custome will be left off and amended: yet not doubting of the effect, by the religious inclination of my Country when just reasons shall be shewed therefore, (although some delight to be obstinate, and because they were bred up in errors, they will not be wiser than their Fathers, but together live and dye in them, yea and condemne that light that others have, because they thinke their darkenesse better) both to annoy'd and amend them: but to accomplish that, hic labor huc opus erat, this was a taske lay somewhat heavy on me to undergoe; and took up no small time to finish, howsoever Master Iohnsons agility could easily wade through it, and his younger shoulders carry away greater burdens; for saith he heavy taskes are best borne by them that are least able, but his quicke speed may conclude with this adage Canis festinans caecos parit catullos: but how and in what sort it is done I leave to judicious censure, not to sharpe toothed and tongued selfe-gnawing envy, that will traduce all others workes to magnifie their owne; for mine owne part, although I boast not of great learning, such as might better have illustrated this worke, yet seeing my genius hath ever driven me to these studies, and my many yeares I thinke hath given me a little more experience, being so long versed thereabout, I hope my time hath not beene ill spent if well taken both in the detection and direction, or also that it will prove more usefull and certaine in rem publicam Botanicam then some others have gone before me, yet if any after me can without envy, having younger and clearer eyes and more setled judgement withall, amend ought that I have set amisse, or not fully declared, per me licet. To the Reader.

Disastrous times, but far more wretched and perverse men, have so far prevailed against my intended purpose and promise to bring this Work to the public view of all, that their extreme covetousness had almost deprived my Country of the enjoyment of it. But having at last—though after long delay and much trouble—broken through all obstacles opposing it, it has at last come forth into the light. And although through the revolution of time it has changed its title (that is, from a Physical Garden of Simples to a Theater of Plants), yet it has not changed its nature; rather it has gained more matter through the expansion, intending to exclude many things that were not proper to it, including a whole class of things that need not be told. For finding in my profession that many slips and errors had crept in and become attached to it, it stirred up in me a desire, having weighed them rightly, seriously to consider how such a habitual custom might be corrected and amended—not doubting of the outcome, given the religious disposition of my Country, once just reasons are shown for it (although some delight in being obstinate, and because they were bred up in errors, will not be wiser than their fathers, but live and die together in them, and even condemn the light that others have, thinking their own darkness better) both to correct the errors and amend them. But to accomplish this was indeed heavy labor for me—this was a task that weighed rather heavily upon me to undertake, and it took no small time to finish. However Master Johnson's agility could easily make his way through it, and his younger shoulders could carry away greater burdens; for as he says, heavy tasks are best borne by those least able to bear them, but his quick speed may conclude with the adage 'the hasty dog produces blind puppies' [Canis festinans caecos parit catullos]. But how, and in what manner, this has been done, I leave to judicious judgment, not to sharp-toothed and self-gnawing envy, which will slander all other works in order to magnify its own. For my own part, although I do not boast of great learning, such as might have better illustrated this work, yet seeing that my inclination has always driven me to these studies, and my many years I think have given me a little more experience, having been so long versed in this subject, I hope my time has not been ill spent, if it is taken well both in its exposition and its guidance—or also that it will prove more useful and reliable to the Botanical commonwealth than some others who have gone before me. Yet if anyone coming after me, without envy, having younger and clearer eyes and a more settled judgment, can amend anything that I have set down amiss, or not fully declared, they have my leave to do so. I know that whoever shall run through as many Fields, Woods, Hills, etc. as this work includes, and shall not stumble at any point, he shall be to me a great Apollo, and I will crown him with such a garland as neither his predecessors nor his successors have ever worn or shall wear. Yet let not an overly presumptuous spirit malign or threaten the Author if he has exposed some of their errors, as if they alone were free from fault, or thought themselves better than Theophrastus, Dioscorides, Galen, Pliny, etc. among the Ancients; or Tragus, Matthiolus, Clusius, Lobel, Bauhinus, among the Moderns—whose slips and errors I likewise expose, who, no doubt, if now alive, being sensibly touched, would rather embrace than spurn the very stone that struck them. One more round with Merret in a Bookseller's shop, for I must not overspend more coin that would try the world's patience, because I have not followed Gerard's method of assigning letters to the several virtues of the Plants, and must therefore be vilified as if no other method were comparable to it. I truly say...

To Englands chiefest Herbarist, Master John Parkinson.

Worthy Sir,
I Have given (as was due) many thankes to my learned good friend Dr. Bainbridge, for communicating to me the sight and perusall of your chargeable, industrious, judicious, usefull, Herculean Botanicall labours. The Commonwealth of learning, particularly the Tribe of Physitians, Apothecaries, Chirurgians, the Court of Nobles, and Gentles, of all who love knowledge, delight, and the honour and good of their Country, owe thankes to you, a Benefactour to the publique, to your Nation, to many millions of particular persons, to the present and succeeding ages. A Triumphall evergreene Lawrell crowne is due to you, for mastering such difficulties, for conquering the great enemyes of a civill World, Ignorance and Barbarisme, for saving so many Citizens of your owne Country, from danger, diseases, destruction, by your carefull understanding directions, for proper fit remedies, in such a rationall pleasing way. Oxford and England are happy in the foundation of a specious illustrious physicke Garden compleately beautifully walled, and gated, now in levelling, and planting, with the charges and expences of thousands by the many wayes Honourable Earle of Danby, the furnishing and enriching whereof, and of many a glorious Temple, withall usefull delightfull plants will be the better expedited by your painefull happy satisfying Worke.

Tho. Clayton, His Majesties professor of Physicke, Oxon.


To the excellent Herbarist M. John Parkinson.

Sir,
I Am a stranger to your selfe, but not to your learned and elaborate volumnes. I have with delight and admiration surveyed your Theatrum Botanicum, a specious, and stately Fabrique, collected and composed with excessive paines, and charges, exquisite Art, and judgement; wherein, may at once be seene, whatsoever (worth th' observing) lyeth dispersed in the severall Botanique monuments of former Ages, and the present: It being indeed, a select Defloration of them all: enriched, and beautifyed with new discoveries (at home and abroad, so far as both th' Indies) of many rare Plants, Herbes, and Flowers. It is a curious portraict and description of th' Earths flowred mantle, the Botanique Pandect, and the Herbarists Oracle, a rich Magazin of soveraigne Medicines, physicall experiments, and other rarities. And which I may not omit. It is (not without th' influence of some benigne Constellation) an Auspicious designe of our Oxford Garden, which being (by the Munificence of the Honorable Founder) once finished, will be the eyes... of most delightfull, and ravishing objects; another Paradise. Such (Sir) is your merit, and the vote of me that is sincerely,

Your affectionate friend,
John Bainbridge,
Doctor of Physique, and
Professor of Astronomy, Oxon.

To the Worthy Apothecary and Herbarist, Master John Parkinson.

Worthy Sir,

You have built us a Botanic Theater, with such excellent skill and advantage to the viewer, that at one view he commands the prospect of both Hemispheres, and all their plants in the pride of beauty, arranged in their proper orders, adorning the Hills, Plains, Valleys, Meadows, Woods, and Banks, with such a world of shapes and colours, so delightful to the eye, so winning upon the rational Soul which feeds on rarities! That we cannot hope for a more complete Paradise upon earth, till Nature has found a new Rib for more variety; what can be added to this I do not see; nor is it (I believe) yet known to the best Artists who have made search.
Thus he judged.

Jacob Sprad, Doctor of Medicine, Oxford.

Tribute to the Botanical Theatre of John Parkinson.

Let Greece no longer see her Cratevas, Andreas, Dioscorides, accustomed to admire only her own; behold, from the farthest West, and from Britain, wholly divided from the whole world, there arises for us now, at long last, a wished-for other Sun of Botanists, who has outshone all others with his own light, and, like a dwarf lifted upon the shoulders of giants, has seen more than the rest. Nor does he begrudge this to the learned world; he has arranged all things in better order, and digested them with more accurate method, gathering into one what others had set down briefly and scattered, and has laid it before you, Reader, to be viewed with that same understanding, and so arranged it that even the greatest masses of matter, through order and method, become as it were agreeable in small compass. Let the age of our forefathers and our own be silent concerning Tragus, Matthiolus, Fuchsius, Gesner, Dodonaeus, Lobelius, and any others of whatever kind; Parkinson alone stands in the place of them all, a British Pillar, to whom one may truly inscribe 'Nothing further.' Concerning whom you might well swear that, by rare good fortune, the spirit of all botanists—both ancient and modern—has migrated into one. This tribute of praise to the work, a token of friendship to its author, and a testimony of esteem, not so much out of love as in obedience to truth, has been paid. L.M.

John Mauritius.

Salve, Salve, venerande Senex,
Qui genius, corculum, medulla, coryphæus Botanicorum cluis.

In hæc studia impulit,
Imo vi traxit,
Industria, laborque indefessus perfectum dedit.

Sed nostræ simul, posteræque ætati pie prospiceres,
Opus hoc doctum, Iupiter & laboriosum

Spretis interim & insuper habitis vitæ omnibus fere delinimentis,
Tanquam Ulysses alter,
Obstructis auribus ad Syrenum cantum,
Scyllam Charybdimque voluptatis lucrique præternavigasti,
Quæ vere sunt mortalium in hoc vitæ solo,
Scopuli, Syrtes, Symplegades,
Ut totum te hisce studiis immergeres.
Tanquam Alexander alter,
Controversiarum Botanicarum nodos plusquam Gordios
Aut feliciter enodasti,
Aut fortiter saltem dissecuisti.
Hinc merito vivus volitas per ora virum.
I, perge, perge Floræ supreme mysta
De re literaria bene porro mereri,
Studia hæc ad metam evehere,
Perenne nomen, decusque tuum ultra supraque invidiam provehere,
Qui priscis palmam eripuisti
Invidiam æqualium & posterorum haud facile vitabis
De opere, ut de Demosthene olim antiquitas,
Quo longius eo melius jure dixerim:
Cuius unica laus admiratio,
Idque tuum maximum Elogium.

Another.

Hail, hail, venerable old man,
who art known as the very soul, the darling, the marrow, the chief of botanists.
Whom nature and thine own genius
drove into these studies,
nay, rather dragged thee by force,
and whose unwearied industry and labor brought to perfection.
But lest thou shouldst sing only for the Muses and thyself,
but rather piously provide for our own age and for posterity as well,
this learned and, by heaven, laborious work
thou hast wrought out with the utmost study and unrelenting toil,
meanwhile having spurned and set aside almost all the allurements of life,
like another Ulysses,
with ears stopped against the song of the Sirens,
thou hast sailed past the Scylla and Charybdis of pleasure and of gain,
which truly are, upon this shore of mortal life,
the rocks, the quicksands, the clashing rocks [Symplegades],
so that thou mightest wholly immerse thyself in these studies.
Like another Alexander,
the knots of botanical controversies, more tangled than the Gordian knot,
thou hast either happily untied,
or at least bravely cut through.
Hence deservedly, while yet living, thou flyest upon the lips of men.
Go, proceed, proceed, thou highest priest of Flora,
to deserve ever better of the world of letters,
to carry these studies to their goal,
to advance thy lasting name and thy honor beyond and above envy,
thou who hast snatched the palm from the ancients.
Thou wilt hardly escape the envy of thy equals and of posterity
for this work — as antiquity once said of Demosthenes,
the further [it is judged], the better, I might rightly say:
whose sole praise is admiration,
and that is thy greatest eulogy.
To a friend, concerning these his studies, concerning his country, concerning himself, of blessed memory.
He gives, dedicates, and consecrates this [work] gladly, deservedly [D.D.C.L.M., abbreviation uncertain].

MY Age of Verfe is out, what then? shall I
Be silent, and not open in this cry
And generall applause? that have more cause
Then some that crowded in; nor shall the lawes
Of friendship draw me from the right way
Of bare and naked truth, and force me say,
In Court civility, more then what I thinke.
Such compliment is on the very brinke
Of flattery, and destroyes the very soule
And essence of true friendship, makes it a foole
Commerce of mutuall sordid ends, which is
The Panacea of humane miseries.
But whether now, my Muse? t'was not my end
To treate of friendship, but to praise a friend.
This weary worke of thy unwearyed braine
Shall doe't for me, and save my further paine.
But soft, that's onely for the Authour, shall
I give nought to the Worke, which gives thee all
Whatsoere it hath here from us, because 'tis such
As like good wine, it doth require no bush?
It were indeed not needfull, if that all

And gentle invitation; as in trade

My age of writing verse is past — what then? Shall I be silent, and not join this outcry and general applause, when I have more cause to do so than some who pushed themselves in? Nor shall the laws of friendship draw me from the straight path of plain and naked truth, and make me speak more in courtly civility than what I truly think. To my old Friend and the King's Herbarist, Mr. John Parkinson, in praise of his Theatrum Botanicum

Phoebus (the sun) has lashed fifty times through the zodiac signs, since you began this jubilee of lines. And now it is published; and shall swiftly scour through dark oblivion until the world's last hour. From the fragrant ashes of Antiquity it springs Phoenix-like, and this shall be the last to die. And if old Dodonaeus [the herbalist] were alive again, here he would wonder, and gain more knowledge. Caspar the Swiss (Bauhin) and Mathiolus the Tuscan shall veil themselves before your Book. Here is more than grows in the Dutch (Batavian) ground; and more than is found in the Paduan Garden; or by the flourishing riverside of Oxford's Physic Garden, by which brave Magdalen's Cherwell still shall glide. Montpellier's flowery meadows yield to you; more is in your leaves than we see on their beds. Yet your rich Work, which we peruse and use, the unwary common folk may rashly abuse. This was not your intent; yet your good pains prostitute noble Physic unto swains (common rustics). Yet still enjoy your Ground, and we your Book, on which Posterity shall ever look. Lodge in your high bed; and at your bed's feet your Plants shall all meet on their moist pallets. From them to you I will transplant that name, for such must be your fame. Keep your Hesperides (garden), may your herbs bloom still with you, never blasted by frost. And seeing that by your hands the day is won, no night of Age shall cloud bright 'Parke-in-sun' (a pun on Parkinson's name).

There is some controversie among Writers concerning this plant, in three or foure particular matters: first, for the etymologie or derivation of the word: some thinking it to be derived from the Greeke word Baso, and the Latine agere, that is to make hast, from the speedy springing of the seed (which is usually within three or foure dayes, if it be a hot and dry time without raine, for moysture turneth it into a gelly, as any one may see, that will looke on it after it hath taken wet) which is written with an h. Secondly, as some thinke, from the Greeke word Ozo, which signifieth to smell, or give a favour, as commonly taken in the worst sence as in the best; and so would have the word to be Ocimon, of the sweet smell thereof. Thirdly, whether it should be Ocimum, as it is to be found in divers ancient Writers, or Ocymum. Fourthly, what Ocimum is of the ancient Writers, for by divers it is taken to be that kinde of graine called Fagopyrum, or Tragopyrum, in English Buckwheate, or else a kinde of medley of Corne or Pulse sowne together, as many ancient Writers have set it downe, as shall be shewed in his proper place, whereunto I shall referre you. And lastly, about the vertues as shall be shewed presently, it is called by the latter Greeke Writers, Basilicon, Basilicum, because the smell thereof being so excellent, is meete for a Kings house. The first two sorts of these Basils are by all Authors so called, as I doe. The second is the same Ocimum that Theophrastus Alpinus saith groweth in the Gardens of Alexandria in Egypt. The third is so called by Lobel and others. The fourth is onely set forth in the great Booke of the Bishop of Eystet his garden: the fift is called Hispanicum, by Camerarius and Tabernaemonta

28  Chap.12.                    Theatrum Botanicum.                    Tribe I.

1. Pseudodictamnus.  Bastard Dittany.        2. Pseudodictamnus alter Pona. Another Bastard Dittany.

withall. The first Bastard Dittany groweth in many places, as Dioscorides saith, and as Lobel saith he understood by some Italians on Monte... neere Pisa and Ligorne in the Florentine Dominions. It is sufficient frequent in many places of Italy in their Gardens, for we have had the seed thereof among others very often from thence, and abideth well in our Gardens also: the last, as Pona in his Italian Baldus saith, groweth in the Iland Cerigo, and brought from thence to Signor Contarini to Padua to furnish his Garden.

The Time.
The true Dittany (as I find) hardly flowreth with us at all, and when it doth, it is very late, not bringing any seed, but Dioscorides (as it is found in the old Copies extant) writeth that it beareth neither flower nor seed, even as he had said before of Nardus montana, but Matthiolus defendeth him, saying, that it was most likely to be the slippe or error of the Writers that set downe often for compares, that is fert or profert, for confert, as thus, nec flores, nec fructum, vel semen fert, or profert, for nec flores, nec fructum, vel semen confert, for Theophrastus saith, lib.9. cap.16. Flos foliorum non ramorum, nec fructus est, and Virgil and others (although Pliny following the corrupted text of Dioscorides, saith it beareth no flowers, nor seed, nor stalke, whereof it is a wonder, having borrowed so much out of Theophrastus, which acknowledgeth it) doe remember the flowers of Dittany, and so doth Galen also in the Emplastrum de Dittamno, whereof Damocrates, as he saith, gave him the receit. The first Bastard Dittany flowreth with us all the latter part of the Summer, but seldome giveth any good seed. The last hath not as yet beene seene in England.

The Names.
It is called in Greeke ... Pulegium sylvestre, by Dioscorides ... by Theophrastus ... some also Aromon and Sinemon, in Latine also Dittamus and Dittamnum, ... Cornarius ... quod virtute quovis in Sanctae mulierum facilis partus promittat, aut dolores praeses sedat, Dioscorides & Theophrastus: the first is called by all Writers Dittamnus or Dittamnum Creticum, or Tictamum, or Dittamnum Creticum: the second likewise is called by all Writers Pseudodittamnus, or Pseudodittamnus, or Pseudodittamnum: Anguillara saith it is called by the Greekes now a dayes Calamintha: Pona would make it to be the Gnaphalium of Dioscorides: the last is only set out by Pona, who taketh it to bee the Dittamnum alterum, of Theophrastus and Dioscorides. The Arabians call it Melisamfe, Anrgen, Araba or Buri, the Italians Dittamo, and other Nations much thereafter according to their Dialect, and we in English Dittany, but not Dittander, as some too foolishly would make it.

The Vertues.
It is availeable as Dioscorides saith, for all the purposes that the planted or garden Pennyroyall is used, but with farre more efficacy, for it not onely expelleth the dead child being drunke, but being applied unto the place (as also a pessary of the same thereof) taken hot, or burnt, and taken underneath: the juyce hath a purging quality applyed with Barley meale: it draweth forth thornes out of the feete, or any other part of the body being applyed to the place: for it is reported that the wild Goates in Candy, being wounded by the Hunters with arrowes, doe by eating this hearbe drive them forth, and are thereby cured. It is held to be very profitable for those that are wounded.

36 Chap.14. Theatrum Botanicum. Tribe I.

Chap. XIIII.
Calamintha, Calamint, or Mountaine Mint.

Although divers Authors doe confound Calamint (calling it Cattmint) with Nep, which is more properly called Catmint, yet I thinke it better to intreat of them a part, then to joyne them both in one Chapter.

1. Calamintha vulgaris. Common Calamint.
The ordinary Calamint that groweth usually abroad in the dry grounds with us, is a small hearbe seldome rising above a foot high, with square hoary, and wooddy stalkes, and two small hoary leaves set at a joynt, about the bignesse of Marjerome, or not much larger, a little dented about the edges, and of a very fierce and quick scent, as the whole heath is: the flowers stand at severall spaces of the stalkes, from the middle almost upwards, which are small and gaping like unto those of Mints, and of a pale bluish colour, after which follow small round blackish seeds; the root is small and wooddy, with divers small springs spreading within the ground, and dyeth not, but abideth many yeares.
There is another of this sort which is like unto it in all things, but somewhat lesser, differing chiefly in the flowers which are not so large by the halfe, which noteth it to be a differing species.

2. Calamintha montana praestantior. The greatest Calamint, or Mountaine Mint.
This sweet Calamint riseth up to be a foot and a halfe high, with his square hard, and hoary stalkes, which are many and slenderer than those of the wild Mints, whereon are set at every joynt two small and somewhat round leaves, deeply dented about the edges, yet larger than those of the former wilde kinde, being somewhat hairy, and not so hoary, but rather of a sad greene colour, of a very sweet scent, not strong or headie as the other; the flowers are gaping, and like the other, but larger, and of a purple colour, after which commeth the seed, which is blacke, small, and round, somewhat like unto Puslain seed; the root is wooddy, but abideth and shooteth forth new branches every yeare.

3. Calamintha altera odore Pulegii foliis maculosis. Spotted Calamint.
This spotted Calamint differeth not much from our ordinary wild Calamint, but that it groweth not so great and high, having square hard hoary stalkes, and hoary leaves thereon like it, but spotted here and there, and of a strong scent like unto Penny-royall; the flowers grow in the same manner, but smaller, and of a pale purplish colour.

4. Calamintha minor incana. Small Calamint.
This hoary small Calamint hath small low and slender hoary stalkes not above a foot high, whereon are set two leaves at a joynt, as in the other sorts, but smaller and more hoary, even smaller than the least, both stalke and the flowers are very small, but like the last, and of a lesse heady scent.

5. Calamintha aquatica verticillata sive aquatica Belgarum Lobelii. Field Calamint with whorled coronets.
This small Field Calamint sendeth forth divers square hoary stalkes full of joynts, and two small and almost round hoary leaves set thereat up to the toppes, somewhat like unto the leaves of Penny-royall, or a quicke and sharpe, yet sweet scent like thereunto also: towards the toppes of the stalkes and branches stand with the leaves many purplish flowers divers set together in a whorle or coronet: the root is small and abideth long, not perishing after seed time.

The Place.
The first groweth on heaths and upland dry grounds in many places of the land: the second on the Bergamo hills, where Tragus, and on the hills neere Verona in Italy, and on the Rocky shadowie cliffs of Savoy or Province in France, as also in Germany, and other places, and in England also, as Lobel saith he observed. The third Pena saith he found on certaine Hills in Lombardy, and in sundry places of our owne Land, yet seldome spared. The fourth Camerarius saith he had the seed from Candy. The last groweth in divers fields of our owne Land, as well in moist medowes, as plowed grounds.

The Time.
They doe all flower in July, and their seed is quickly ripe afterwards.

The Names.
It is called in Greeke kalaminthe quasi bona et amita Mentha, a good or profitable Mint. The first is called Calamintha vulgaris or montana vulgaris by most Authors: and the lesser of this sort Bauhinus calleth Calamintha vulgaris minore flore. The second is called of Lobel, Camerarius, and others Calamintha montana praestantior, as the best of all the sorts of Calamints, in English as it is in the title. Gerard giveth the figure of this for Serandonis, or Salvia agrestis.

Chapter 14 of Theatrum Botanicum, on Calamint, or Mountain Mint.

Although divers authors confound Calamint (calling it Catmint) with Nep, which is more properly called Catmint, yet I think it better to treat of them separately, rather than to join them both into one chapter.

1. Common Calamint. The ordinary Calamint growing commonly in dry ground with us is a small herb, seldom rising above a foot high, with square, hoary, woody stalks and two small hoary leaves at each joint, about the size of marjoram or a little larger, slightly toothed at the edges, and having a very sharp, pungent scent throughout the plant. The flowers appear at intervals along the upper parts of the stalks, small and gaping like those of mints, of a pale bluish colour, followed by small round blackish seeds. The root is small and woody, with many small spreading fibers, and it does not die but persists for many years. There is another variety like it in all respects but somewhat smaller, differing chiefly in the flowers, which are half the size, marking it as a distinct species.

2. The Greatest Calamint, or Mountain Mint. This sweet calamint grows to about a foot and a half high, with square, hard, hoary stalks, more numerous and slenderer than the wild mints, bearing at each joint two small, roundish leaves deeply toothed at the edges, larger than those of the former wild kind, somewhat hairy but less hoary, of a darker green colour, with a very sweet (not strong or heady) scent. The flowers are gaping, like the others but larger, and purple in colour, followed by small, round, black seed like purslane seed. The root is woody but persists and sends up new shoots each year.

3. Spotted Calamint. This does not differ much from the ordinary wild calamint, except it grows smaller, with square, hard, hoary stalks and hoary leaves like it, but spotted here and there, with a strong scent like pennyroyal. The flowers grow similarly but are smaller and of a pale purplish colour.

4. Small Calamint. This hoary, small calamint has low, slender, hoary stalks not above a foot high, with two leaves at each joint as in the other kinds, but smaller and more hoary — even smaller than the least of the others. Both the stalks and flowers are very small, similar to the last kind, but with a less heady scent.

5. Field Calamint with whorled coronets (Dutch water calamint, per Lobel). This small field calamint sends up several square, hoary, jointed stalks with small, nearly round hoary leaves reaching to the tops, somewhat resembling pennyroyal leaves, with a sharp yet sweet scent similar to it. Near the tops of the stalks, clusters of purplish flowers grow together in a whorl or coronet. The root is small and persists long, not dying after seeding.

The Place. The first grows on heaths and dry upland ground in many parts of the country. The second grows on the Bergamo hills (according to Tragus), and on hills near Verona in Italy, and on the rocky shaded cliffs of Savoy or Provence in France, as well as in Germany and elsewhere, and also in England, as Lobel observed. The third, Pena says, he found on certain hills in Lombardy, and in various places in our own land, though rarely. The fourth, Camerarius says, he obtained the seed from Crete (Candy). The last grows in various fields of our own country, in moist meadows as well as plowed ground.

The Time. They all flower in July, and their seed ripens quickly afterward.

The Names. It is called in Greek 'kalaminthe,' as if 'good or beneficial mint.' The first is called by most authors Calamintha vulgaris or montana vulgaris; the lesser variety is called by Bauhin Calamintha vulgaris with the smaller flower. The second is called by Lobel, Camerarius, and others Calamintha montana praestantior, being the best of all the calamints — hence the English name given in the title. Gerard's figure of this plant is given under 'Serandonis' or wild sage.

9. Aster Virginianus luteus alter minor. Another yellow Starwort of Virginia.
The other yellow Starwort of Virginia grows up with only one upright small round stiff stalk, four or five feet high, bearing two fair green long shining leaves at every joint, dented about the edges, but smaller than the former, standing on small foot-stalks, and somewhat hard to the touch; at every joint with the leaves on both sides, from the very bottom come forth branches, half a yard long at least, with similar leaves on them; at the top of each stalk and branch stands one flower, whose green small round button beneath it has several small green leaves on the head thereof, out of which breaks the flower, consisting of a dozen yellow small and long leaves surrounding a middle deep yellow center; though I and some others have had it growing with us, yet it has flowered and seeded only with Master Tradescant at South Lambeth. Because it flowers late, we have not yet observed the seed well; the root is composed of sundry white and long hardish strings, with small fibers on them, and lasts several years, increasing at the sides, but the top perishes to the ground, shooting new heads every year.

10. Aster Conyzoides. Fleabane-like Starwort.
This kind of Starwort has long and narrow leaves growing on branched stalks, which are a foot high, growing singly without order; the flowers grow singly at the top of every stalk and branch, composed of dusky yellow leaves, with a browner center in the middle turning into down, which along with the small seed is carried away by the wind: the root is thready.
We have had from Virginia another sort of this kind, very like it, but with smaller flowers.

Among these I must recall the Aichimenes of America, a plant most nearly resembling white Bryony, as shall be seen when we come to it, and some other foreign plants as well.

1. The common white Bryony or wild Vine.

The white Bryony or wild Vine, which grows commonly in the wild, climbing up over hedges, sends forth many long, rough, very tender branches at first, bearing many rough, broad leaves, for the most part cut into five divisions, shaped much like a vine leaf but smaller, rougher, and of a whitish or hoary green colour. It spreads far over trees or bushes or whatever stands next to it, twining with small tendrils that grow out at the leaf-joints. At these same joints, especially toward the tops of the branches, arises a long stalk bearing many whitish flowers gathered together in a long cluster, each consisting of five small petals spread open like a star. The first groweth in many places of this Kingdome, in woods and untilled places, and serveth among the shrubbes for hedges; the second Clusius found both in the upper and the lower Hungary, upon those hills nearest to the Alpes, as also in Moravia in the woods there. The last was found by Clusius also, in a wood in that part of Hungary that is called Interamnis, and which the Germanes call Winterschlandt beyond the river Dravus.

The Time.

They doe all flower about May, and their berries are ripe in September.

The Names.

This is generally by most Writers called Evonymus, and taken to be the true Evonymus of Theophrastus in his 3. cap. ultimo, and which he calleth Tetragonia translated Quadrangularia by Gaza in this Booke and fift Chapter; but there are diverse, and Lugdunensis with them, doe rather judge it to be Euonymus, which Gesner in his Epistles, and Clusius in his history of Plants, thinke to be Ledum, and is by Clusius called Ledum Alpinum, (which I have remembred before in the former chapter) Ulisses Aldrovandus Nomina Aromatum, as Gesner in description mentioneth also, and is probable to be Chamaerhododendros Alpina odora of Pena and Lobel in their Adversaria, and which Anselm in his Observations calleth Balsamum Alpinum: but Clusius thewreth plainely, that it cannot agree therewith, not having the foure square head or huske. It hath beene corruptly called Anonymus of diverse, instead of Euonymus, as Cordus Hist. saith, Tragus mistaking it called it Carpinus. It is called also Fusanum and Fusaria, because the Italians called it Fusaro, as being used by Turners and others, to make spindles for spinning wheeles and other things, by Barbarous Euonymus vulgaris grana rubentibus. The second is called by Clusius Euonymus alter, quae from by Camerarius and Tabermontanus Euonymus Pannonicus, and by Barbinus Euonymus grana nigris. The third called Euonymus five latifolus by Clusius and all others. It is called in English Spindle tree, Prickewood, and Prickwood, and in some countries of this land Dogwood, and might from the forme of the berrie well be called Square berried tree. The Italians call it Fusano, the French Fusin, and Fusaro depressa, the Germans Spindelbaum, the Dutch Papenhaut.

The Vertues.

This is seldome used in Physicke with us for to helpe any disease, yet it is found by experience that foure kernells will purge both by vomiting and by the stoole, causing much choller and flegme to be voided, and from him diverse others have said that the leaves hereof are pernicious and deadly to Sheepe and Goates, unlesse they be purged by Anschin (which word is not well knowne what it meaneth) donaeus interpreting it, that they should be purged upward and downeward, and others understanding it should be purged by want or abstinence from meate, Dalechampius as Lugdunensis reciteth it, avoweth that saying of Theophrastus, to be hurtfull to Goates by his owne experience, whi few flockes of Goates upon the shrubbes that grew with this, but none of them touched it, and that they refused to eat it being offered them, but Clusius saith the cleane contrary, that hee understood the Goates in Hungary did greatly desire the leaves thereof, and tooke no harme thereby, and that the Hungarians in their language call this tree Kechke rago fa, id est capis rosa arbor, the Goates Rose tree, so diverse be the writings and opinions of men, whereof in many other things we have sufficient experience.

Chapter 55.
Rubia major, Madder.

Besides the cultivated and wild Madder, both of which were known to the ancients, there are nowadays many other kinds discovered which were not known to them, both of the greater and lesser sort — some growing on mountains, some in meadows and pastures, and some by the seaside. But because I would not overload one chapter with too many of them, let me here show you only the greater sorts, and in the following chapter the lesser ones.

1. Garden Madder (cultivated Rubia major).
The Garden Madder puts forth many very long, weak, four-square reddish stalks trailing far along the ground, very rough or hairy (which is why Pliny calls it 'spinosus,' prickly), and full of joints. At each of these joints grow several long, somewhat narrow leaves arranged like a star or the rowel of a spur around the stalks, rough and hairy afterward. Toward the tops come many small pale yellow flowers, after which appear small round heads — green at first, reddish later, and black when fully ripe — containing the seed. The root is not very thick, but extremely long, reaching down half a man's depth into the ground; it is red and very clear-colored while fresh, spreading in various directions.

2. Wild Madder.
The wild Madder resembles the cultivated kind in all respects, except that its stalks are smaller and do not spread as far, nor are they as rough or hairy. The leaves are smaller, the flowers white, and the root grows larger but is not as red or as clear-colored as that of the garden kind.

3. Wild Madder with longer leaves.
This wild Madder has several round, jointed stalks, two or three feet long or thereabouts, somewhat smooth, or at least not as rough as the other wild sort. The leaves growing at the joints are somewhat rough, narrower and longer than the other kind, seven or eight to a whorl. At the tops of the stalks stand many white flowers, each made of four small petals, which turn into small round seeds like the other kind; the root is smaller but red like the former.
